Kāverī
(‘daughter of the king Kavera’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism has always considered rivers and mountains as sacred spots since they are conducive to the practice of spiritual disciplines.
Kāverī (often called ‘Dakṣīṇagaṅgā’) is one of the seven most sacred rivers of India included in the मन्त्र invoking the seven rivers, at the time of ritualistic worship.
Taking its birth in the Brahmagiri hill of the district of Koḍagu (or Coorg) in Karnataka, it flows in the south-easterly direction through the Mysore and the Tanjavur (Tanjore) districts of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu states, ultimately merging in the Bay of Bengal near the small town Kaveripattinam. Its total length is 760 kms. (475 miles).
The place where it emerges out of the womb of earth is called Talakāverī. It is 39 kms. (24 miles) from the central town of Madikeri and 8 kms. (5 miles) from the little town of Bhāgamaṇḍala. The place of its emergence named Kuṇḍige is just a little pool 0.6 metre squre (2 feet square). To its north is a small maṇṭapa (temple-like structure) about 1.2 meters (4 ft) in height. The water of the Kuṇḍige gets accumulated in a small tank and then flows out under the ground.
Every year, during Tulāsaṅkramaṇa (i.e., when the sun enters the Libra, generally during October), at a particular moment of the day, there is a sudden bursting forth of water in the small pond Kuṇḍige. On this day, thousands of people gather there to offer worship to the goddess कावेरी, bathe in the tank and also carry home a little of the holy water.
There are several stories in the epics and the पुराणस् regarding the river and the river-goddess कावेरी.
She was the foster-daughter (known earlier as Viṣṇumāyā) brought up by the king Kavera and hence called ‘Kāverī’. She was also known as ‘Lopāmudrā’ and was given in मर्रिअगे to the sage अगस्त्य. Once when अगस्त्य was travelling to the south of the country beyond the विन्ध्य mountains, he was carrying her in the form of water in his कमण्डलु (water pot of mendicants) which was upset by a powerful wind near the Sahyādri mountain from where she started flowing as a river.
Other stories are similar but add that she was originally a river flowing in कैलास, the abode of शिव.
A large number of small rivers and rivulets join it at various places. Well-known centres of pilgimage situated on its banks are: श्रीरङ्गम् in Tamil Nadu; श्रीरङ्गपट्टण near Mysore in Karna-taka; Madhyaraṅga temple near Shivana-समुद्र in Karnataka state.
In all these three places which are small islands in the river, there are temples of रङ्गनाथ, an aspect of विष्णु in the reclining posture.
The famous Śaiva temples on its banks are those at चिदम्बरम् and Tañjāvur (Bṛhadīśvara महादेव). Mention may be made of the Jambukeśvara temple near श्रीरङ्गम् also.
Tirujñāna सम्बन्धर्, the well-known Śaiva saint, was born on the bank of कावेरी. Kamban, the famous poet, is said to have composed his Rāmāyaṇa in Tamil, on the bank of this river.

Kavaṣa Ailūṣa
(‘Kavaṣa, the son of Ilūṣa’)
------------------------------------------
One of the characteristics of the Hindu scriptures is frankness and directness whether it concerns good or evil. Also, if an idea considered as right was later found to be wrong, it was unceremoniously discarded and replaced with the right one. The story of कवष ऐलूष is such an illustration.
Kavaṣa, the son of Ilūṣa was born to a śūdra woman who was a slave and hence was castigated by the contemporary society of ब्राह्मण sages. He could neither enter a place of sacrifice nor even have social contacts with the ब्राह्मणस् of his times.
Once, when some sages like the Bhṛgus and the Aṅgirasas were performing a सत्त्रयाग, they found that कवष ऐलूष was also sitting there amongst them. When they discovered this, they promptly evicted him from there, and forcibly banished him to a desert. However, when Kavaṣa was languishing there, by divine grace, a Vedic सूक्त was revealed to him. This is known as the Aponaptrīya hymn (Ṛgveda 10.30.1-15) and is used in Somayāgas. It is chanted by the होतृ priest. The presiding deities of water were pleased with him. As a result, the river सरस्वती started circumambulating him and the place became fertile.
Learning of this miracle, the sages who were performing the सत्त्रयाग hurriedly came to him, apologised to him for their arrogance and invited him to participate in their sacrifice as an honoured priest.
This story appears in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa (8.19) and also in the Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa (12.3).
Another Kavaṣa is mentioned in the Ṛgveda (7.18.12) as one who was overthrown by इन्द्र. He was probably the priest of the tribe named ‘Vaikarṇa’.
